I work in the IT field and had to train my "offshore" replacements. What follows is a different story, describing a wholly different Prajeet.

Prajeet horror story time!

I was working for a large financial firm supporting their internal Microsoft Exchange e-mail infrastructure, and we had a project of some sort that required additional resources for completion. Our manager elected to employ a Prajeet.

A few days after arriving he was disappointed to learn two fundamental facts:

We were not running the latest version of Exchange at that moment;

and

He was going to be working a ticket queue to free up the actual engineers to finish the project-related work.

I was the junior engineer in the group, so our manager foisted the Prajeet on me. I briefly showed him how to operate the queue, and (foolishly) left him to himself.

Time passed, and he proceeds to complain over the course of a relatively short period of time that this "assignment" wasn't going to "get him ahead" in his career, and how he just didn't understand why we were content with the situation. This quickly became tiresome for all within earshot of him.

Days pass, and we start getting calls about people losing access to long-standing meetings and conference rooms in their calendars. We look into these requests and realize that the Prajeet has handled all of the users or the rooms that were affected in these cases. It turns out that he had granted access to individual users to the conference rooms as an Owner, which allows the users to cancel any standing meetings in those rooms and set their own. He also proceeded to destroy the auto-attendant, which is a script that brokers scheduling of the rooms in an automated fashion. I inquired with the Prajeet as to why he did this, and his answer was "The customer asked for it, and the customer is always right." I almost had a stroke on the spot.

The first rule in support is that you always refuse to do what someone is asking for before investigating further and making an informed decision. Then, and only then, do you grant (or deny) the requests. This fool did not understand that these were shared resources that had to be shared between 32,000 people.

Needless to say, we kept him far from anything that could be even remotely data destructive until he decided to voluntarily leave.

I gave up on Prajeets after this. 1 week of repairing what this fool broke was my penance.
